method: Authorized single recovery read; each claim is captured as printed and retains source-page provenance.

facts: Minerals are classified into metallic, non-metallic and fuel minerals.
Metallic minerals listed include iron, copper, manganese, nickel, gold, platinum, silver, chromite, tungsten, cobalt, zinc, lead and tin.
Ferrous metallic minerals are defined as iron-bearing and listed as iron, manganese, chromite, tungsten, nickel and cobalt.
Non-ferrous metallic minerals are listed as gold, zinc, lead, aluminium, silver and tin.
Precious metals are listed as gold, silver and platinum.
Non-metallic minerals are listed as limestone, dolomite, mica, gypsum, nitrate and potash.
Fuel minerals are listed as petroleum, coal, lignite, uranium, thorium and natural gas.
India is printed fifth in iron-ore reserves after Australia, Brazil, Russia and China.
India is printed fourth in iron-ore production after Australia, China and Brazil and second in crude-steel production after China.

Hematite is printed as red, 72 percent iron, widespread in Dharwar and Kadapa rocks, with Odisha 34 percent and Jharkhand 23 percent resource shares and deposits also in Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Goa and Andhra Pradesh.
Hematite is described as the second-hardest mineral after diamond and called superior iron ore; Sweden, the United States and Russia are listed for magnetite-grade comparison.

Magnetite is printed as black, 60 to 70 percent iron, occurring in Dharwar and Kadapa rocks, with Karnataka 72 percent and Andhra Pradesh 13 percent resource shares and occurrences also in Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Goa and Assam.
Limonite is printed as brown or yellow, 40 to 60 percent iron, relatively low quality and found in Raniganj, Mirzapur and Himachal Pradesh.
Siderite is printed as under 40 percent iron, difficult to smelt, carbonate iron or bog ore, and occurring in Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh.
A national iron-ore resource figure of 33,276 million tonnes is printed, with Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka and Goa named.
visuals: Green chapter-title banner and hierarchical printed list
correction_flags: Ferrous/non-ferrous classification is inconsistent: tungsten, nickel and cobalt are not iron-bearing in the simple chemical sense.
Hematite is not the second-hardest mineral after diamond; this is a factual error.
Iron-content ranges, reserves and rankings require year-tagged IBM data.
Siderite is not synonymous with bog ore; classifications need correction.

facts: Printed iron-ore production shares are Odisha 60 percent, Chhattisgarh 14 percent, Karnataka 13 percent and Jharkhand 11 percent.
Jharkhand iron-ore areas listed are Singhbhum district, Noamundi, Notaburu, Gua, Pansiraburu, Budaburu and Kiriburu.
Odisha iron-ore areas listed are Keonjhar, Talcher, Mayurbhanj, Sundargarh, Diringburu, Sambalpur and Koraput.
Chhattisgarh iron-ore areas listed are Bailadila hills, Dalli-Rajhara, Ari Dongri, Rowghat and Chandrapur.
Karnataka iron-ore areas listed are Chitradurga, Ballari, Chikkamagaluru, Baba Budan hills, Kemmanagundi and Kudremukh.
Goa iron-ore areas listed are Bicholim, Sanguem or Sirigao and Mapusa.
Andhra Pradesh iron-ore areas listed are Anantapur, Kadapa, Guntur, Krishna, Kurnool, Nellore, with hematite in Prakasam and magnetite or siderite in Prakasam.
Japan is said to import about three-fourths of its iron ore and South Korea and European countries are also named as importers.
Iron uses listed include machinery, transport vehicles, satellite rockets, transformers, synthetic ammonia catalysts, pigments and rubber-polishing products.
Manganese is described as obtained from pyrolusite and psilomelane and mainly from Dharwar rocks.
Printed manganese resources total 406 million tonnes, distributed Odisha 44 percent, Karnataka 22, Madhya Pradesh 12, Maharashtra 7, Goa 7 and Andhra Pradesh 4 percent.
Printed annual manganese production is 28 lakh tonnes, with Odisha 34 percent, Madhya Pradesh 28, Maharashtra 21, Karnataka 11 and Andhra Pradesh 10 percent.
Andhra Pradesh manganese production is listed in Vizianagaram and Srikakulam.
Manganese ore is printed as containing 12 to 14 percent iron and used in bleaching powder, glass, photography, leather, fertilizers and gauze industries.
Chromium is introduced as obtained from chromite and used in stainless steel, with 18 percent chromium and 8 percent nickel printed for stainless steel.
Chromium is linked with corrosion resistance, aircraft, electrical and chemical industries, and a melting point of 2623 degrees Celsius.
Chromium use in aircraft and nuclear industries and ferrochrome production is stated, with 68 percent chromic oxide printed for chromite used in ferroalloys.

Indian chromite resources are printed as 144 million tonnes, concentrated in Odisha or Sukinda, with Manipur, Nagaland, Karnataka and Jharkhand also listed; production is printed as Odisha 99 percent followed by Karnataka and Maharashtra.
correction_flags: All percentage shares and totals are date-sensitive.
Several locality spellings are uncertain and need IBM/GSI normalization.
The printed manganese production shares sum above 100 percent and are internally inconsistent.
The stainless-steel composition is one common grade, not a universal definition.

facts: Bauxite is described as named after Les Baux in France in 1821 and as a red or brown, oily or clay-like ore.
Aluminium is obtained from bauxite through hydrated oxide and alumina stages; the ore is described as light, inexpensive and easily worked.
Bauxite or aluminium uses are printed as electricity 48 percent, automobiles and transport 15 percent, construction 13 percent, machinery 7 percent and packing 4 percent.
India is called a major aluminium producer and aluminium recycling is stated to reduce raw-material use.
India is printed seventh in bauxite resources, with a major Deccan Trap deposit at Chota Nagpur.
A national bauxite resource figure of 2,462 million tonnes is printed.

Major bauxite state localities listed are Odisha at Kalahandi and Koraput, Andhra Pradesh at Visakhapatnam or East Godavari, Gujarat at Jamnagar, Kaira and Kutch, Jharkhand at Ranchi, Lohardaga, Palamu and Gumla, Maharashtra at Kolhapur, and Chhattisgarh at Bilaspur and Raipur.
Printed bauxite production shares are Odisha 50 percent, Gujarat 24, Jharkhand 9 and Chhattisgarh 8 percent.
A yellow box says the Central Mines and Minerals Regulation Act was made in 1957.
Copper is described as a red-brown metal occurring as cuprite and malachite and as an excellent conductor.
Copper is linked with electrical engineering and is printed as using 45 percent of world output in electrical work and offices.
Brass is correctly described as copper plus zinc and bronze as copper plus tin; German silver is printed as copper, zinc and nickel.

Indian copper deposits are listed in Rajasthan at Khetri-Ajmer-Alwar-Bhilwara, Madhya Pradesh at Balaghat, Jharkhand or Singhbhum, Andhra Pradesh at Agnigundala and other Guntur/Kurnool/Kadapa/Anantapur localities.
Chile, Peru and Australia are described as leading copper-reserve countries, and Chile and Peru as leading producers.

Printed Indian copper production is concentrated in Madhya Pradesh at Malanjkhand and Rajasthan at Khetri/Kolihan, followed by Jharkhand at Surda, Kendadih and Rakha; Chile, Indonesia, Australia and Peru are named as import sources.
Zinc is introduced as sphalerite-derived zinc sulphate or ore and also from calamine, zincite and willemite.
Printed zinc uses are galvanizing 55 percent, batteries 24 percent and alloys 10 percent.
correction_flags: The statute name should be Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957.
Bauxite rank, total, state shares and use shares need year-tagged verification.
Bauxite formation and Chota Nagpur wording are oversimplified.
Copper and zinc use shares and production locations require IBM year labels.

facts: World copper resources are ranked Australia, Russia, South Africa and the United States; world copper production is ranked China, Russia, Australia, Canada and the United States as printed.

A note prints newly discovered 2017 Rajasthan copper deposits of 11.48 crore tonnes in Banswara, Udaipur and Sikar districts, about 300 feet deep, with mica minerals in Sikar's Neem Ka Thana and lead deposits in Jaipur.
Platinum is described as used in jewellery, car air bags, televisions, computer monitors and cancer-treatment drugs.

Platinum and palladium are described as concentrated in South Africa and Russia; Indian resources are printed Odisha 67 percent or Keonjhar Boula-Nuasahi, Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, with production Odisha, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh.
Silver is described as obtained from argentite by electrolysis and commonly associated with lead, zinc and copper ores.
Silver uses listed include alloys, electroplating, photography, photovoltaic cells, solder and medicine; Peru and Australia are named as leading producers, while Mexico and China lead output.
Indian silver deposits are listed in Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Andhra Pradesh or Guntur-Kurnool, and Telangana; production is printed for Rajasthan and Jharkhand.
Diamond is described as crystalline carbon obtained from anthracite coal as printed, used for cutting and polishing, and historically linked to Surat.
Indian diamond occurrences are listed in Madhya Pradesh or Panna, Andhra Pradesh at Vajrakarur kimberlite and Banganapalle, Kadapa, Guntur and Krishna, and Chhattisgarh.
Diamond production is printed only in Madhya Pradesh or Panna, with AMD exploration at Kalyandurg in Anantapur and Bharat Gold Mines work around Vajrakarur.
Nickel is described as obtained from pentlandite, used as an alloy in stainless steel, catalysts, electroplating, rechargeable batteries, paints and rockets.
Indian nickel resources and production are printed in Odisha, Jharkhand and Nagaland.
correction_flags: World copper rankings are implausible or outdated and need USGS verification.
Diamond is not obtained from anthracite coal; this is a major factual error.
Silver extraction is not universally by electrolysis and argentite is only one ore.
All resource, discovery and production claims require dates and official sources.

facts: World diamond resources are ranked Australia, Russia, South Africa and the United States, while production is ranked China, Russia, Australia, Canada and the United States as printed.
A 2017 note prints 11.48 crore tonnes of Rajasthan copper deposits around Banswara, Udaipur and Sikar, at a depth of about 300 feet, with associated Sikar mica and Jaipur lead claims.
Platinum and palladium are linked with jewellery, automotive air bags, televisions, computer monitors and cancer-treatment medicines.
Printed Indian platinum resources are Odisha 67 percent at Boula-Nuasahi in Keonjhar, Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu; production is listed in Odisha, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh.
Silver is described as argentite-derived by electrolysis and commonly associated with lead, zinc and copper deposits.
Silver uses listed are alloying, electroplating, photography, photovoltaic cells, soldering and medicine; Peru and Australia are named as resource leaders and Mexico and China as production leaders.
Silver deposits are listed in Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Andhra Pradesh at Guntur and Kurnool, and Telangana; production in Rajasthan and Jharkhand.
Diamond is described as pentlandite-derived in the printed continuation, but the surrounding passage mixes diamond and nickel descriptions.
Nickel is explicitly described as pentlandite-derived, important in stainless steel, and used in catalysts, electroplating, rechargeable batteries, paints and rockets.
Nickel deposits and production are listed in Odisha, Jharkhand and Nagaland.
Diamond is further described as formerly from anthracite coal, with occurrences at Panna, Vajrakarur, Banganapalle, Kadapa, Guntur, Krishna and Chhattisgarh and production only at Panna.
Diamond exploration is attributed to AMD at Kalyandurg and Bharat Gold Mines at Vajrakarur.
correction_flags: Page 447 visibly repeats or overlaps text from page 446 and mixes diamond with nickel; content must be disentangled.
Diamond-from-anthracite and diamond-from-pentlandite implications are false.
Platinum air-bag use wording is likely a confusion with automotive catalysts and safety-system components.
World rankings and all Indian resource/production claims require current authoritative verification.
